name: Crushed mother-of-pearl face powder

lead: Mother-of-pearl is the iridescent inner shell layer of some molluscs, and pearls are made of the same material. Ground to powder, it has been applied to the face and skin and taken in traditional medicine to brighten the complexion.

Its sheen comes from thin aragonite platelets whose thickness is close to the wavelength of visible light. Cosmetic mica and synthetic pearl pigments now provide similar shimmer, while traditional pearl powder remains in some Asian skincare.

paras: Historically applied as a dusting powder or mixed into creams and masks to add luminosity and lighten the look of skin. Modern products blend it into creams and powders.

A 19th-century source warned of a pale, sickly appearance and possible skin harm. Wikipedia notes that excessive oral doses may cause calcium toxicity. Trade in some shell sources is regulated under CITES.

angle.text: As a powder it adds a visible pearly sheen to the skin. Traditional users also apply it with the aim of brightening and fading marks.

lead: Crushed mother-of-pearl (nacre) face powder is a pearlescent cosmetic made by grinding the inner layer of shells. It has been used to give the face a luminous, paler finish.

Pearl powder use in China is recorded from at least 320 AD, and the Ming-era Bencao Gangmu credited it with renewing skin and fading sun damage and age spots [1]. In India, Ayurvedic texts used it, and in 19th-century Europe some women used it as a skin whitener [1].

A 1996 Chinese review reported that, in laboratory studies on animals, the powder of sea pearl, mother-of-pearl and freshwater pearl showed tonic, anti-aging and anti-radiation actions [2]. Nacre itself is an aragonite and biopolymer composite [3].
infobox: Regulated under CITES for some sources [3]

paras: Nacre consists of hexagonal aragonite platelets, roughly 10-20 micrometres wide and half a micrometre thick, separated by thin organic layers of chitin and proteins [3]. The platelet thickness is close to the wavelength of visible light, producing structural iridescence [3].

Pearl powder has been used as medicine and cosmetic in China since at least 320 AD; Wu Zetian is said to have used it [1]. Narahari, a Kashmiri physician around 1240, described it as a strength tonic [1]. In the 1800s some European women used it to whiten skin, though one source of the time warned it left a pale, sickly hue [1].

Pearl powder is widely believed to improve skin appearance and is used in creams, masks and powders; claims include acne help and support for collagen and wound healing, which Wikipedia attributes largely to primary and historical sources [1]. Traditional Chinese medicine uses it as an anti-inflammatory and calming agent [1].
No studies found. A 1996 review summarised animal experiments in rats and mice reporting tonic and anti-aging actions of pearl and mother-of-pearl powder [2].
